passage: Sit, Parul. Your Vasudha Nani is going to tell you something, because you're making the same face I made at twenty. In my second year of college I planned to sell mango pickle at the Diwali mela. My friend's plan was simple: set up a table, sell what we could. Mine was grand. The principal's wife would taste it and tell the staff, the local paper would write about us, and by Holi we'd have orders from Nagpur. I could picture every step, even the headline. That picture made my plan feel more real than hers, not less. It rained on mela day, the principal's wife never came, and we sold eleven jars from the simple table under the stairs. Every extra piece of my story was another thing that had to happen. Now tell me your startup plan again. The short version.

With three hours left in the college hackathon and the Wi-Fi dropping every twenty minutes, Chandrika spread her hands over the table. "Here's how we win. We finish all four features, the live demo runs first try, the judge from the logistics company is on our panel, she loves the route-map idea, and she offers us internships on the spot."

"Every bit of that has to work out. The Wi-Fi alone..."
The screen froze again. Chandrika stared at the spinning circle, then at her list of four features. "Okay," she muttered, "but mine's a better story."
"It's a better story," Amandeep agreed. "It's a worse plan."

"Bhabhi, listen. It's all planned." Irfan spread his notebook on the dining table. "I top this semester, Professor Rao picks me for her project, she writes my letter, I get the scholarship to Singapore, the visa comes before August, and I start in September."
Pooja put down the tea. "And if you only top? Not Singapore?"

Mentor's note, final-year project review, 14 March.
Shreya presented her group's plan for the campus water-saving project today. It was a lovely story: the hostel wardens would agree in week one, a local firm would donate sensors, the student union would run an awareness drive, and the results would be published by May. She clearly believed every step. Pranav, her teammate, proposed a smaller version: fix the leaking taps in one hostel and measure the water used. Shreya called it "too small to be real". I asked the group to write each step on a card and put a rough chance next to it. Seeing the cards laid out in a row, Shreya went quiet. After the meeting she stayed back and asked if she could start with Pranav's hostel and build from there. I said yes.

qa.q: What smaller version did Pranav propose?
qa.a: Pranav proposed fixing the leaking taps in one hostel and measuring the water used.

qa.a: Shreya felt proud and attached to the full story; its many connected steps made success feel vivid and believable, so a plain plan seemed less real.

qa.q: Why did the card exercise help, and what could Shreya do with it next?
qa.a: Putting a chance beside each step showed how many things all had to go right; Shreya can start small, as she chose to, and add steps once each one works.

qa.a: Pranav would likely feel respected and relieved that the smaller idea was finally taken seriously.

12 October, night.
Tejas and I finally planned the Diwali trip. My version is perfect: 5:40 train to Lonavala, reach by 8, hike to the fort, lunch at the dhaba Tejas's cousin swears by, sunset at the point, last train home. I can picture every minute. Tejas wanted something simpler: one hike, back by afternoon, no timings. I said that sounds like a plan that won't happen, while mine obviously will, because it's all worked out.
Then Tejas made me count: train on time, both of us awake at 5, no rain, the dhaba open on a festival day, the fort path not packed, the last train not full. Six things. Hmm. Mine still feels more real. But real and likely might not be the same thing. Writing both plans in here to see which one we end up doing.
Eshaan

passage: In Karnal, Simran had been planning the college cultural fest for two weeks. Her plan was beautiful: the MLA would inaugurate it, a famous folk singer from Chandigarh would perform for free, the local sweet shop would sponsor food, three nearby colleges would send teams, and the local TV channel would cover it. Every detail made her more excited. It felt so real. Jyoti, the treasurer, read it on a Sunday afternoon on the college steps. "Simran, what happens if the singer says no?" "She won't." "And if the MLA is busy?" Simran's smile slipped. "Every one of these has to happen for your plan to work," Jyoti said gently. "Five yeses. What if we plan for two?" Simran sat down. Her beautiful plan suddenly looked fragile. That evening they wrote Plan B: local college bands, a canteen stall, and the MLA as a bonus.

qa.q: What did Jyoti suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Planning for fewer yeses, like two instead of five, because every added condition makes the whole plan less likely to work.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel pointing out the weak spots?

passage: In a café in Copenhagen, Lars laid out his startup plan for Ines on a napkin. "We build the app by March. Then a big bike company notices us. Then they partner with us. Then the city puts us on its website. Then we get investors." He drew arrows between every step, grinning. The more he talked, the more real it felt to him. Ines, who studied statistics, didn't laugh. "How likely is each step?" "I don't know. Maybe half?" She did the maths on the napkin. "Half, times half, times half, times half, times half. That's about three in a hundred that all of it happens." Lars stared. "But it sounds so good when I say it all." "That's the trap," Ines said. "Every 'and then' makes it sound better and makes it less likely." He crossed out four arrows and circled the first step.

qa.q: What chance did Ines work out for the whole plan?
qa.a: About three in a hundred that all of it happens.

qa.q: Why did the plan feel more real the more Lars talked?
qa.a: Each vivid step made Lars feel more excited and sure, even though adding steps made the whole plan less likely.

qa.q: What did Lars do after Ines's maths, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: He crossed out four arrows and circled the first step, focusing on what he can do now instead of a long chain of hopes.

qa.q: How does Ines see Lars's plan?
qa.a: Ines sees each added step as another thing that must go right, making it sound better but less likely.

"Here's how it goes," she said. "The paint shop sponsors us, the band from Shillong says yes, the auditorium is free on the 14th, it doesn't rain, two thousand people come, and we make enough to fund next year too."
